newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria top economic figures sketch strategic plan.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria top economic figures sketch strategic plan.

text.p: Many of Nigeria's top economic figures met in the capital on Wednesday to find a plan to restore wealth to what should be one of Africa's richest countries.
A 172-member committee has the job of creating "Vision 2010", a strategic plan to develop the economy.
Its members include the heads of the multinationals that pump Nigeria's crude oil as well as bankers, businessmen, government officials and traditional chiefs.
"The people who have come here today are people who clearly have other things to do, that must be some measure of how seriously Vision 2010 is taken," said one of the organisers.
"We are in a no-lose situation. At worst nothing comes of it, at best there could be a great benefit for Nigeria," Mobil Corp's Nigerian unit managing director Jim Massey told Reuters.

Behind closed doors, the group discussed areas that had emerged from an economic summit in September which partly inspired "Vision 2010", including improving living standards through better education and health facilities as well as economic growth and deregulation.

Announcing "Vision 2010" at the economic summit, military ruler General Sani Abacha flagged it as necessary for Nigeria to achieve growth by adopting a development plan similar to Asian nations, notably Malaysia.
So far Nigeria has shown little sign of springing into life as an African Tiger.

Although among the 10 largest crude-oil-producing nations in the world, most of Nigeria's 100 million people live in poverty with poor services bequeathed by a succession of governments whose grand words have come to little.
Nigeria's economic woes deepened in 1993 when the military annulled elections that would have brought to an end a decade of army rule and restored democracy.
Abacha took over as head of state in the ensuing chaos from Ernest Shonekan, now chairman of "Vision 2010", an advocate of economic deregulation.
Alleged human rights abuses and lack of democracy have pushed Nigeria to the status of pariah in the eyes of the West.

But even as international condemnation reached a high point with last year's execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists, serious economic sanctions against Nigeria barely reached the agenda.
Most of the two million barrels of crude oil pumped per day go to the United States, while former colonial power Britain and other European nations also have significant trade interests in Nigeria.

On the political front, the outside world remains suspicious of Abacha's plan to restore civilian rule by October 1998. But his economic policy since 1995 has won plaudits both at home and abroad for bringing annual inflation down to around 30 percent from above 70 percent in little more than a year.
"Even as people are turning away from Africa we can't ignore Nigeria, mostly because of oil, but also because of its potential as a market," said one Western diplomat.
"Vision 2010 is interesting, as long as by the time they have finished talking the world hasn't already moved another step ahead."
